L1752: # Microsoft commits to sweeping AI privacy rules for students. Will other tech giants follow?
L1753: 
L1754: cite177†Image: Teachers work with AI on their laptops during the Charleston County School District Charleston Educator Symposium Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in North Charleston, S.C. (AP Photo/Mic Smith)†dims.apnews.com L1755:

L1775:   * cite182†Email L1776:   * cite183†X†twitter.com L1777:   * cite184†LinkedIn L1778:   * cite185†Bluesky†bsky.app L1779:   * cite186†Flipboard†share.flipboard.com L1780:   * cite187†Pinterest†pinterest.com L1781:   * cite188†Reddit†www.reddit.com L1782: Millions of students every day turn to cite189†AI chatbots for help with schoolwork, emotional support and personal advice — often unaware of where their conversations and other personal information end up.
L1783: 
L1784: How that data is used — and schools’ role in protecting it — is a growing concern for educators, parents and kids as artificial intelligence becomes a ubiquitous part of the school day, embedded in many of the classroom tools students are required to use.
L1785: As the school year started, the country’s two largest school districts, New York City and Los Angeles, announced they were cite190†putting the brakes on student use of AI for one year, as they study how to best incorporate the technology into education.
L1786: In response to a growing AI and screentime backlash, cite191†Microsoft announced last week it had agreed to adopt guardrails and privacy standards for its AI in schools, as negotiated with the American Federation of Teachers, the country’s second-largest teachers union.
L1787: The safety provisions in the agreement are meaningful, but the standards will only be effective if all AI companies, especially the tech giants, sign on, said Josh Golin, executive director of online safety nonprofit Fairplay. He said the agreement sidesteps the question of whether cite192†AI products even belong in classrooms, or at what age they should be introduced.
L1788: “I worry that a high-profile framework like this will be misunderstood and schools will think, ‘If they’re doing a good job on data privacy and safety, then that means we should be using the tool,’” Golin said.
L1789: The AFT said the agreement, which is legally binding and requires third-party audits for compliance, could set an industry standard. Two other leading AI companies, cite193†OpenAI and cite194†Anthropic , said they also were discussing safety and privacy pacts with the AFT. But cite195†Google , the dominant provider of education technology for America’s schools, has not said whether it plans to offer similar protections.

L1806: cite198†21 L1807: ## Agreement puts limits on using student data for training AI
L1808: 
L1809: As part of the cite199†wide-ranging agreement†www.aft.org , Microsoft says it will not use student or educator data to train AI systems, apart from a narrow exception for data that could help protect students. It says the data it collects cannot be sold, used for advertising or used for product development.
L1810: The agreement prohibits any use of AI companions or features “designed to foster emotional attachment or dependency” and to keep students engaged for longer than a learning task requires. It also includes a range of audit and transparency measures that require the company to disclose to families, in plain language, how its tools work.
L1811: “This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” Brad Smith, Microsoft’s vice chair and president, said in a statement. The standards will apply to all schools that Microsoft has contracts with starting Nov. 1, he said.
L1812: 
L1813: Read More
L1814: AFT President Randi Weingarten called the agreement the “first of its kind” and an important step to setting an industry standard in the absence of federal and state legislation on AI in schools.
L1815: 
L1816: “We want parents to have control of their kids’ education. We want educators to have control of kids’ education, not ed tech. And that’s what this agreement is,” Weingarten said.
L1817: She spoke at a joint news conference with Smith at the headquarters of the United Federation of Teachers, the AFT’s New York City affiliate. The headquarters is home to AFT’s National Academy for AI Instruction for teachers, which cite200†launched a year ago backed by $23 million from Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic.
L1818: Along with their yearlong AI moratorium, the school systems for New York City and Los Angeles plan extensive audits of their education technology contracts and AI tools, with a focus on data privacy, transparency and accountability. The ban in New York City applies to all elementary and middle school students, while in Los Angeles it extends through high school.
L1819: ## The teachers union also has courted Google and AI companies
L1820: 
L1821: Weingarten said she contacted Google directly to tell them about the agreement before making it public, in hopes the company would become a signatory.
L1822: 
L1823: The company has not responded to a request for comment from The Associated Press on whether it plans to offer similar protections.
L1824: “Is Google going to embrace this framework? That is a huge question,” said Golin, the online safety nonprofit chief. He noted schools also use thousands of AI-driven educational technology products produced by smaller companies.
L1825: Google found itself at the center of controversy over AI in schools when it announced in August it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. The company says Google Classroom is used by 150 million teachers and students worldwide.
L1826: Critics decried Google’s move as an escalation of the race between tech giants to make inroads in schools and win over the next generation of AI users. The AI addition to Classroom only affects schools that allow student access to its Gemini app or Gemini Notebook, but it marks a major shift. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.
L1827: 
L1828: Weingarten said she is also in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic, which both issued public praise for the agreement.
L1829: OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, called it an “important milestone for AI safety and privacy in schools.” The company has been working with AFT, it said in a statement, “and we look forward to finalizing our own agreement.”
L1830: 
L1831: Anthropic, the maker of Claude, said in a statement, “We applaud all efforts to drive responsible AI use in education.” The company said it was working with AFT to shape “a gold standard for safety and privacy.”
L1832: ## The standards shift the burden on privacy to companies
L1833: 
L1834: Experts in data privacy say the new standards could help shape the conversation that schools have with AI providers, whether a school is a Microsoft customer or not.
L1835: “What I’m hopeful about is that this takes some of the pressure off individual school districts to negotiate with large tech companies,” said Elizabeth Laird, director at the Center for Democracy and Technology. Until now, the negotiating power of schools to secure privacy protections from tech firms often depended on financial clout. “I think this standard makes progress toward not having that type of inequity across school districts.”
L1836: Laird commended the agreement for going “above and beyond” what is legally required for vendors working with schools. For instance, Microsoft has committed not to use sensitive data that many companies leverage, such as information about gender, race, age, ZIP code that can be used to identify a person even if their name is removed.
L1837: But until others sign on, Laird said, the agreement highlights how difficult it is to set AI standards in the absence of legislation. It also emphasizes that the burden of protecting student privacy should fall on tech companies — not on parents, students or schools.
L1838: 
L1839: Microsoft’s Smith noted that tech companies have been late to accept that.
L1840: “We all know there are important discussions and debates all across the country, about when AI should be used in schools, how it should be used, for what purpose,” Smith said. “It is our role, even our responsibility, to ensure that AI is provided in a form that teachers and kids and parents can trust.”

L8: # AFT, UFT and Microsoft announce ‘National AI Safety & Privacy Standard’ for schools to protect students, families and educators
L9: ## Landmark agreement hands parents and educators control through legally enforceable guardrails, builds on NYC schools’ screen and AI ban
L10: 
L11:   * cite4†Microsoft Source L12: NEW YORK — Sept. 9, 2026 — After months of intense negotiations and in the absence of any meaningful federal and state rules governing artificial intelligence in schools, AFT President Randi Weingarten, United Federation of Teachers President Michael Mulgrew, and Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith today announced a “cite5†National AI Safety & Privacy Standard†cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com ” establishing legally enforceable protections to ensure the safety of students, families and educators.
L13: The first-of-its-kind cite6†agreement†www.aft.org on the heels of New York City Public Schools’ screens and AI ban, ensures that tech companies cannot use student data to train AI, students can never be tracked, AI cannot make decisions without human oversight, and companies must give educators and parents transparency and plain-language answers about how their tools work. U.S.
L14: school districts can incorporate these protections directly into their Microsoft customer agreements, making them contractually enforceable.
L15: “We have forged a hard-fought, iron-clad privacy agreement with real teeth that protects students and families, because no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work,” Weingarten said. “We can get angrier and angrier, or we can act decisively; anything less than legally enforceable provisions is simply a wish list.”
L16: Weingarten continued, “This agreement ensures three foundational goals: protect the privacy and data of children, give schools real control over AI tools in the classroom, and provide transparency and information to parents. And with New York City adopting our framework to ban screens and AI use in the younger years, this agreement adds to the momentum around online safety for kids and educators.”
L17: In a May speech, “cite7†Devices Down, Eyes Up, Hands-On†www.aft.org ,” Weingarten flagged her fight for an enforceable data privacy standard and called for a total screen ban from kindergarten through second grade, a ban on student-facing AI in elementary school and a ban on social companion chat bots for students under 16.
L18: A similar framework has been adopted by the Los Angeles Unified School District, the New York State United Teachers (the AFT’s state affiliate), and last week, New York City Public Schools and Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
L19: “This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” said Microsoft’s Smith.
L20: 
L21: At its core, the agreement turns shared principles into clear, enforceable protections centered on three priorities:
L22:   * Protecting privacy: Educators, parents and students can have confidence that data remains theirs. Student and educator data will not be used to train AI models, sold or repurposed, and schools will maintain control over how data is used, retained and deleted.
L23:   * Enhancing safety: Students and educators are protected by strong security, safeguards and human oversight. AI systems must be designed to avoid harmful or manipulative experiences, protect sensitive information, and meet rigorous standards for security, accountability and responsible use.
L24:   * Providing transparency and control: Families can expect clear, accessible information about how AI is being used in schools and their safeguards, including what data is collected and what protections are in place. Schools retain control over when and how AI is used, and companies need to communicate clearly about product changes, risks and controls.
L25: “Educators are stepping in to do what we do best: protect our students. This agreement gives families and school districts the information and privacy protections they have been demanding, and it empowers school districts to end agreements and seek damages from bad actors who break the rules.
L26: It starts to level the playing field in a competitive, ever-changing arena that lacks the guardrails our children and school communities need,” said the UFT’s Mulgrew, who leads the 200,000-member New York City AFT affiliate.
L27: In 2024, the AFT released its “cite8†Commonsense Guardrails for Using Advanced Technology in Schools†www.aft.org ,” which established nine core principles to ensure students and families were informed and protected. And last year, it announced the creation of the cite9†National Academy for AI Instruction†www.aft.org , which enables educators to access training on the use and misuse of AI tools rather than being treated like an afterthought, as so often happens with changes in education technology.
L28: Led by educators, the academy allows teachers not only to become proficient with the emerging technology but to be diligent about student safety and privacy.
L29: “HIPAA and FERPA never envisioned the advent of AI,” Weingarten said, “and in the absence of those protections, tech companies need to take responsibility for the products they create and market to students, educators and communities.”
L30: 
L31: A fact sheet on the agreement can be viewed cite10†here†aka.ms , and the full agreement can be viewed cite6†here†www.aft.org .
L32: Microsoft (Nasdaq “MSFT” @microsoft) creates platforms and tools powered by AI to deliver innovative solutions that meet the evolving needs of our customers. The technology company is committed to making AI available broadly and doing so responsibly, with a mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.

L2@P0: Preamble — Why This Agreement Exists
L3@P0: This Memorandum of Agreement exists for one reason: children come first.
L4@P0: Students are not products. Teachers are not beta testers. And schools are not a source for data
L5@P0: collection or experiments. When artificial intelligence tools enter a classroom, they bring
L6@P0: enormous potential, and equally enormous responsibility. This agreement sets one of the
L7@P0: highest standards for how that responsibility must be met.

L9@P0: national initiative dedicated to equipping educators with the knowledge, skills, and support to
L10@P0: use artificial intelligence effectively and responsibly in teaching and learning.

L42@P1: As used in this Standard:

L44@P1: including but not limited to: names, student ID numbers, grades, disciplinary records,
L45@P1: prompts entered into AI Provider Educational Product, AI-generated outputs tied to a
L46@P1: student, behavioral patterns, device identifiers, location data, memory files, audio or
L47@P1: visual data, and metadata. This definition is intentionally broad. When in doubt about
L48@P1: whether something is Student Data, treat it as Student Data.
L49@P1: • "Covered Data" means Student Data plus any data belonging to or generated by
L50@P1: educators, administrators, or an EDU Customer (including the Academy) when using AI
L51@P1: Provider Educational Products. Covered Data does not include Telemetry Data (as
L52@P1: defined below).
L53@P1: • “Telemetry Data” means technical and operational data generated through the use or
L54@P1: operation of the AI Provider Educational Products that has been de-identified so that it
L55@P1: cannot reasonably be used to identify, relate to, describe, or be linked to an individual
L56@P1: student, or educator. Telemetry Data may be associated with an EDU Customer solely
L57@P1: for security, reliability, debugging, capacity planning, service health, aggregate
L58@P1: performance monitoring, and to make product improvements. Telemetry Data may not
L59@P1: be used, directly or indirectly, for generative-model training, student profiling, individual
L60@P1: student user personalization of AI outputs, advertising, marketing, behavioral inference,
L61@P1: or the creation or enhancement of profiles concerning individual users.
